chapter: The 1920s road: dance style and management
title: Knowing Bert Williams and Jack Johnson; minstrels and plantation shows
summary: He met Williams and Johnson in New York; earlier black performers were in minstrel shows, not major theatres, and Negro acts were a godsend to vaudeville.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Yeah. I met him after I went to New York. I knew Jack Johnson, too.
Was Bert Williams -- he was performing on the stage prior to you.
Oh, he was before me, sure he was. Sure he was. So was Johnson. There were quite a few on before I was but they

weren't in the business. I hope you can get the understanding that these people were on the stage before me but where were they on the stage? Where were they? If you're talking about a theater, you're not in any theater in the united world unless you are at the Palace or the Paladium as of today and as of 20 years ago. So where were they if they were on the stage? Where were they? You got the minstrels -- you got Huntington's Mighty Minstrels, you got Al G. Fields Minstrels. You got so many minstrels that's going on and plantation shows that went on in years gone by that the theaters weren't taking such acts -- negro acts especially. So the negro acts was like a godsend to that world the same as television was to the picture world. Television was an amplification on pictures. You don't see as many picture theaters today as you did then, 'cause television takes over. After a while, they're going to have something else to take over that, too. You don't know what it is, but there's going to be something
